questions.prompt: How do you turn a component into a Client Component?

options.text: Put the directive "use client" as the first line of its file
Export it from a file named client.tsx

questions.explanation: The "use client" directive at the top of a file marks the client boundary; that file and its imports become Client Components.

questions.prompt: Which are true of Server Components? Select all that apply.

options.text: They can use useState and onClick
They ship no JavaScript to the browser

questions.explanation: Server Components fetch data, use secrets, and ship no JS. State and event handlers require a Client Component.

questions.prompt: A Client Component cannot import a Server Component, but it can render one passed to it as this prop. Name the prop.
questions.explanation: Passing a Server Component as children (a slot) lets server content live inside a client shell without the client importing it.

questions.prompt: You need one interactive button on an otherwise static, data-fetching page. What's the best structure?

options.text: Keep the page a Server Component and make only the button a Client Component
Add "use client" to the whole page
Fetch the data in a useEffect on the client

questions.explanation: Keep the page on the server (for data fetching and less JS) and push only the interactive button to the client.

questions.prompt: Match each capability to where it belongs.
questions.explanation: Data fetching and secrets belong on the server; state, events, and browser APIs belong in Client Components.

questions.prompt: Order how a page with a Client Component becomes interactive.

items.text: Server Components render to HTML on the server
The HTML is sent to the browser and displayed
Hydration attaches interactivity to that component

questions.explanation: The server renders HTML first; then the Client Component's JS loads and hydration wires up its interactivity.
